From the third to fifth ribs to the coracoid process of the scapula
From the acromion to the humerus
e: To produce shoulder flexion, horizontal adduction and internal rotation, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Pectoralis major runs from the sternum, clavicle and upper ribs to the anterior humerus, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce shoulder flexion and internal rotation?
o: From the clavicle to the humerus
From the upper nine ribs to the anterior scapula
From the acromion to the humerus
From the spine of the scapula to the humerus
e: To produce shoulder flexion and internal rotation, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Anterior deltoid runs from the clavicle to the humerus, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce shoulder abduction?
o: From the acromion to the humerus
From the upper nine ribs to the anterior scapula
From the thoracic spine to the scapula
From the scapula to the anterior humerus
e: To produce shoulder abduction, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Lateral (middle) deltoid runs from the acromion to the humerus, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce shoulder extension and external rotation?
o: From the spine of the scapula to the humerus
From the upper nine ribs to the anterior scapula
From the sternum, clavicle and upper ribs to the anterior humerus
From the scapula to the anterior humerus
e: To produce shoulder extension and external rotation, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Posterior deltoid runs from the spine of the scapula to the humerus, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce shoulder internal rotation, adduction and extension?
o: From the scapula to the anterior humerus
From the upper nine ribs to the anterior scapula
From the clavicle to the humerus
From the acromion to the humerus
e: To produce shoulder internal rotation, adduction and extension, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Teres major runs from the scapula to the anterior humerus, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce shoulder external rotation?
o: From the scapula to the posterior humerus
From the thoracic spine to the scapula
From the acromion to the humerus
From the anterior scapula to the anterior humerus
e: To produce shoulder external rotation, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Teres minor runs from the scapula to the posterior humerus, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce shoulder internal rotation?
o: From the anterior scapula to the anterior humerus
From the spine of the scapula to the humerus
From the scapula to the posterior humerus
From the fossa above the spine of the scapula to the top of the humerus
e: To produce shoulder internal rotation, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Subscapularis runs from the anterior scapula to the anterior humerus, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce abduction of the arm?
o: From the fossa above the spine of the scapula to the top of the humerus
From the occipital bone, nuchal ligament and spinous process of C7 to the lateral third of the clavicle and the acromion
From the scapula to the posterior humerus
From the anterior scapula to the anterior humerus
e: To produce abduction of the arm, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Supraspinatus runs from the fossa above the spine of the scapula to the top of the humerus, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce elbow flexion, forearm supination and shoulder flexion?
o: From the scapula to the radial tuberosity
From the scapula and humerus to the ulna
From the medial humerus and ulna to the radius
From the lateral humerus and ulna to the radius
e: To produce elbow flexion, forearm supination and shoulder flexion, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Biceps brachii runs from the scapula to the radial tuberosity, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce elbow extension and shoulder extension?
o: From the scapula and humerus to the ulna
From the humerus to the radius
From the medial humerus and ulna to the radius
From the lateral humerus and ulna to the radius
e: To produce elbow extension and shoulder extension, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Triceps brachii runs from the scapula and humerus to the ulna, which does exactly that.

q: Which attachment pattern would produce elbow flexion?
o: From the humerus to the radius
From the acromion to the humerus
From the scapula and humerus to the ulna
From the lateral humerus and ulna to the radius
e: To produce elbow flexion, the line of pull has to cross the joint on the side that shortens during it. Brachioradialis runs from the humerus to the radius, which does exactly that.

q: Gastrocnemius originates on the posterior femur, above the knee. What follows for a calf raise performed with the knee bent?
o: Gastrocnemius contributes less, so the work shifts towards soleus
Gastrocnemius contributes more, because the knee flexion pre-stretches it
Nothing changes, since both muscles insert on the calcaneus
The Achilles tendon takes the load instead of either muscle
e: Bending the knee brings the femoral origin closer to the calcaneus, slackening gastrocnemius before the movement starts. Soleus originates below the knee on the tibia and fibula, so it is unaffected, which is why a seated calf raise shifts the work towards soleus.

q: Why is it difficult to produce maximal hip extension and maximal knee flexion at the same moment?
o: The hamstrings cross both joints, and both actions shorten them
Reflexes between the hip and knee stop both joints being driven at once
Gluteus maximus inhibits the hamstrings whenever the knee is flexing
Rectus femoris is stretched at both ends and blocks the knee bending
e: Biceps femoris long head, semimembranosus and semitendinosus all run from the ischial tuberosity past the knee. Extending the hip shortens them at one end and flexing the knee shortens them at the other, so the muscle runs out of range. It is why a stiff-legged deadlift and a leg curl train the same muscles in genuinely different ways.

q: Biceps femoris short head originates on the linea aspera of the femur rather than the pelvis. What does that mean it cannot do?
o: Extend the hip
Flex the knee
Externally rotate the tibia
Stabilise the knee
e: A muscle can only act on joints its line of pull crosses. The short head starts on the femur itself, below the hip, so the hip is not in its path at all. It flexes the knee and externally rotates the tibia like the long head, but it is the one part of the hamstring complex that does nothing for hip extension.

q: The long head of triceps brachii originates on the scapula rather than the humerus. What follows for an overhead triceps extension?
o: It is lengthened at the shoulder before the elbow extends
It is switched off, so only the medial and lateral heads work
It becomes a shoulder abductor rather than an elbow extensor
It loses all leverage at the elbow once the arm is overhead
e: Raising the arm overhead moves the scapular origin away from the ulna, putting the long head on stretch before the set begins. That is the argument for overhead variations: the head that crosses the shoulder is the one that is loaded differently by arm position, while the other two heads are unaffected.

q: Biceps brachii originates on the scapula, not the humerus. What does that add to its job list beyond the elbow and forearm?
o: Shoulder flexion
Shoulder abduction
Scapular retraction
Shoulder external rotation
e: Crossing the shoulder gives it a third action. Biceps flexes the elbow, supinates the forearm and assists shoulder flexion.

q: Tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus both insert into the iliotibial band. How do their hip actions compare?
o: They oppose: TFL flexes and internally rotates, glute max the reverse
They are synergists, both extending and externally rotating the hip
They are synergists, both flexing and internally rotating the hip
TFL abducts and glute max adducts, with no rotational difference
e: A shared insertion does not mean a shared action; what matters is where each one starts. TFL comes off the ilium in front of the hip and glute max from behind it, so the same band is tensioned from two opposite directions.

q: Sartorius runs from the iliac bone across the thigh to the medial tibia. Which combination does that diagonal line produce?
o: Hip flexion, external rotation and abduction, with knee flexion
Hip extension, internal rotation and adduction, with knee extension
Hip flexion, internal rotation and adduction, with knee extension
Hip abduction and internal rotation, with knee extension
e: Trace the line and the answer falls out. It starts in front of and outside the hip and finishes inside the knee, so shortening it flexes, externally rotates and abducts the hip while flexing the knee. That is the position of sitting cross-legged, which is where its name comes from: it is the tailor's muscle.

q: Gracilis is the only adductor that reaches past the knee, inserting on the medial tibia. What does that add?
o: It assists knee flexion and tibial internal rotation
It assists knee extension
It produces ankle inversion
It has no action beyond the hip despite the insertion
e: Every other adductor stops on the femur, so it can act only at the hip. Gracilis carries on to the tibia, so it also assists knee flexion and tibial internal rotation.

q: Gluteus medius has anterior and posterior fibres with opposite rotational actions. What produces that split?
o: The fibres lie on either side of the hip's rotation axis
The anterior and posterior fibres have different nerve supplies
The posterior fibres attach to the sacrum rather than the ilium
Only the anterior fibres cross the hip joint itself
e: Both sets abduct, because both run from the ilium down to the greater trochanter. But the anterior fibres lie in front of the rotational axis and the posterior fibres behind it, so one internally rotates and the other externally rotates. One muscle, two opposed jobs, decided by geometry.

q: Adductor magnus is often described as having a hamstring part. Which fibres earn that description and why?
o: The posterior fibres, which extend the hip rather than flex it
The anterior fibres, because they attach nearest the ischium
All of it, because the whole muscle crosses the knee joint
Neither: the name refers only to the muscle's size
e: The posterior fibres run from nearer the ischial tuberosity down the back of the femur, which is the hamstring line of pull. They adduct like the rest of the muscle but extend the hip where the anterior fibres flex it, so the same muscle appears on both sides of the hip action list.

q: External oblique produces contralateral rotation and internal oblique ipsilateral rotation. What explains the difference?
o: Their fibres run in opposite diagonals across the trunk
The external oblique is stronger, so it dominates the direction
Internal oblique attaches to the spine and external oblique does not
The difference is in timing rather than direction
e: External oblique runs downward and forward, internal oblique downward and backward, forming an X across the abdomen. Rotating left uses the right external oblique together with the left internal oblique. They work as diagonal pairs, which is why trunk rotation is never a one-muscle job.

q: Transversus abdominis runs horizontally and inserts into the linea alba. What follows for what it can do?
o: It cannot move the spine at all; it can only compress
It rotates the spine more powerfully than the obliques
It flexes the spine but cannot extend it
It laterally flexes the spine only
e: A line of pull has to cross a joint at an angle to move it. Transversus abdominis wraps round the abdomen into a midline seam, so shortening it draws the waist in and raises intra-abdominal pressure rather than moving the spine.

q: Rectus abdominis has vertical fibres running from pubis to ribs. Why is it a poor rotator despite appearing in the rotation column?
o: Its vertical line of pull sits close to the spine's rotation axis
Its tendinous intersections split it, which prevents rotation
It is too superficial to reach and turn the vertebrae
It rotates only when the obliques are inhibited
e: Flexion is what a vertical anterior line does well: it draws the ribs towards the pubis directly. Rotation needs a diagonal, which is what the obliques supply. The tables list rotation for rectus abdominis, but the geometry says it is a minor contributor.

q: Pectoralis major has clavicular and sternal fibres. What does the split mean in practice?
o: Clavicular fibres suit flexion; sternal fibres adduct from lower down
Clavicular fibres rotate inwards; sternal fibres rotate outwards
Only the sternal fibres actually cross the shoulder joint
The two parts have identical actions but different nerve supplies
e: Both converge on the anterior humerus, but one starts high on the clavicle and the other low on the sternum and ribs. The angle of pull differs, which is the mechanical basis for incline versus flat pressing.

q: Serratus anterior and the rhomboids act on the same bone in opposite directions. What is the pairing?
o: Serratus protracts and rotates it upward; rhomboids do the reverse
Serratus elevates the scapula; the rhomboids depress it
Serratus retracts the scapula; the rhomboids protract it
Both protract it, differing only in the degree of upward rotation
e: Serratus runs from the ribs to the front of the scapula and pulls it forward round the rib cage. The rhomboids run from the thoracic spine to the medial border and pull it back towards the spine, rotating it downward.

q: Supraspinatus and the lateral deltoid both abduct the arm. What distinguishes their contributions?
o: Both work from the start; supraspinatus has better early leverage
The deltoid does all the lifting; supraspinatus only rotates
Supraspinatus works only once the arm is above shoulder height
They are interchangeable, so a cuff problem never affects abduction
e: Both are active from the start of abduction. With the arm at the side the deltoid pulls mostly up along the humerus, so supraspinatus has the better leverage early and presses the humeral head into the socket; 'supraspinatus alone does the first 15 degrees' is a simplification.

q: Latissimus dorsi runs from the lumbar spine, iliac crest and thoracic spine to the anterior humerus. What does that unusual span let it do?
o: Link the arm to the pelvis, so it also controls spinal flexion
Rotate the lumbar spine as its main job, like the obliques
Elevate the scapula and hitch the pelvis on the same side
Act as a hip extensor through a direct femoral attachment
e: Almost nothing else in the body bridges the pelvis to the humerus. That span is why a tight lat limits overhead reach by tethering the arm to the trunk, and why it appears in the spinal deceleration column despite being thought of as an arm muscle.

q: Teres major is sometimes called the lat's little helper. What does it share, and what does it lack?
o: The same shoulder actions, but no spinal or pelvic attachment
The same spinal attachments, but no insertion on the humerus at all
The same shoulder actions, plus retraction of the scapula
The same origin on the pelvis, but the opposite rotation
e: Both insert on the anterior humerus and both extend, adduct and internally rotate the shoulder. Teres major starts on the scapula rather than the spine and pelvis, so it does the arm half of the job without any of the trunk connection.

q: Fibularis longus starts on the lateral fibula but inserts on the medial side of the foot. How does it evert?
o: Its tendon wraps behind the lateral malleolus, which acts as a pulley
Its tendon changes direction inside the ankle joint capsule
It everts only when posterior tibialis relaxes and stops opposing it
Its medial insertion is a naming convention, not a real attachment
e: The straight line from origin to insertion is not the line of pull; the tendon's path is. Wrapping behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot turns a laterally placed muscle into one that pulls the medial side downward, which is eversion. Bony pulleys change actions, so attachments alone can mislead.

q: Posterior tibialis and fibularis longus both attach near the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal, yet oppose each other. Why?
o: They approach from opposite sides of the ankle
One inserts on bone and the other on fascia
Posterior tibialis acts only during the stance phase of gait
Their actions are identical and the tables disagree
e: Posterior tibialis passes behind the medial malleolus and inverts; fibularis longus passes behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot, and everts. Similar insertion region, opposite approach, opposite action.

q: Soleus originates below the knee, on the tibia and fibula. What does that make it well suited to?
o: Postural work at the ankle regardless of knee position
Producing power only when the knee is fully extended
Assisting knee flexion during the swing phase of running
Controlling the arch during pronation
e: Because it does not cross the knee, its length is unaffected by whether you are standing, sitting or squatting. That independence is why it carries much of the continuous, low-level work of holding the body upright over the ankles.

q: Anterior tibialis runs down the front of the shin to the medial cuneiform. What is its most common eccentric job in walking?
o: Lowering the forefoot to the ground after heel strike
Driving plantar flexion at push-off, at the end of stance
Holding the knee extended through the middle of stance
Resisting eversion of the foot throughout the swing phase
e: It accelerates dorsiflexion, so lengthening under load it controls the opposite. After the heel lands, anterior tibialis pays out to lower the forefoot to the ground instead of letting it slap down.

q: Quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest to the 12th rib and lumbar vertebrae. What does shortening it on one side do to the pelvis?
o: Hitches that side of the pelvis up and bends the spine towards it
Drops that side of the pelvis and bends the spine away from it
Rotates the pelvis towards the opposite side, without tilting
Tilts the pelvis forwards, with no movement to either side
e: Either end can be the moving one. Fix the ribs and the pelvis rises on that side; fix the pelvis and the spine bends towards it. Both are the same shortening, and which one you see depends on what is anchored, which is a general rule worth carrying to every muscle.

q: Levator scapulae attaches the cervical spine to the scapula. Why do the tables list two quite different sets of actions for it?
o: Either end can be the anchor, so it moves whichever end is free
It has two separate bellies, each with its own nerve supply
Its action depends on whether the head is already rotated
One set is concentric, and the other belongs to another muscle
e: A muscle pulls both of its ends towards each other, and whichever end is held still acts as the origin. With the shoulder anchored it extends and side-bends the neck; with the neck anchored it elevates and downwardly rotates the scapula.

q: Erector spinae accelerate spinal extension. What are they doing during the lowering phase of a hip hinge?
o: Working mainly isometrically to hold the spine still
Shortening concentrically to drive the trunk down towards the floor
Relaxing, since gravity and the hip muscles produce the movement
Working isometrically only at the very bottom of the hinge
e: In a hip hinge the movement happens at the hips, and the hip extensors lengthen under load. The erector spinae mainly hold the spine's position against gravity, which is isometric work that stops it flexing.

q: Multifidus produces spinal extension and contralateral rotation. What makes it suited to segmental control rather than gross movement?
o: It spans only a few vertebrae, acting segment by segment
It is the largest and strongest of all the spinal extensors
It attaches to the ribs rather than to the vertebrae
It contracts only during rotation, never in extension
e: Short muscles crossing few joints are positioned for fine control rather than large movement, in the same way the rotator cuff is positioned relative to the deltoid. Multifidus is why segmental stability and gross trunk strength are different qualities.

q: Brachialis runs from the humerus to the ulna. Why is it unaffected by whether the forearm is supinated or pronated?
o: The ulna does not rotate as the forearm turns
It is too deep to be influenced by forearm position
It crosses the shoulder, which makes up for the change
Its tendon rotates with the radius to compensate
e: Pronation and supination are the radius crossing over a relatively fixed ulna. Biceps inserts on the radius, so forearm position changes its leverage; brachialis inserts on the ulna and is therefore a pure elbow flexor in any grip. That is the reasoning behind the hammer and reverse curl.

q: Semitendinosus and semimembranosus internally rotate the tibia, while biceps femoris externally rotates it. What explains the split?
o: Biceps femoris inserts laterally, the other two medially
They arise from different parts of the ischial tuberosity
Biceps femoris crosses the hip, and the other two do not
Only biceps femoris crosses the knee joint at all
e: All three descend from the ischium, but they finish on opposite sides of the knee. A medial insertion turns the tibia inward when it shortens; a lateral one turns it outward. Insertion side decides rotation, which is derivable without memorising it.

q: Three of the four quadriceps originate on the femur and one on the pelvis. What single difference does that create?
o: Only rectus femoris can flex the hip
Only rectus femoris can extend the knee
The vasti cannot stabilise the knee
Rectus femoris cannot contribute to knee extension
e: All four converge on the patella and extend the knee. Rectus femoris is the only one whose origin lies above the hip, so it is the only one that crosses two joints and the only one that flexes the hip. Everything distinctive about it follows from that one attachment.

q: Upper trapezius attaches to the occipital bone and C7 at one end and the clavicle and acromion at the other. What two regions can it therefore act on?
o: The cervical spine and the scapula
The cervical spine and the humerus
The scapula and the ribcage
The thoracic spine and the humerus
e: It spans from skull and neck to shoulder girdle, so it appears in both lists: cervical extension, lateral flexion and rotation, and scapular elevation. A muscle that crosses two regions has a job in each, and which one moves depends on which end is anchored.

q: Pectoralis minor runs from the ribs to the coracoid process of the scapula. What does shortening it do?
o: Draws the scapula forward and down into protraction
Draws the scapula back and up, into retraction and elevation
Rotates the humerus inwards at the shoulder joint
Flexes the shoulder by pulling the humerus forward
e: It never touches the humerus, so it cannot move the arm directly. It pulls the coracoid towards the ribs, drawing the scapula forward and down.

q: Which muscle would be lengthening under load during the cocking phase of a throw, as the shoulder externally rotates to its limit?
o: Subscapularis
Infraspinatus
Teres minor
Posterior deltoid
e: External rotation is being produced, so the internal rotators are the ones paying out to control it. Subscapularis is the cuff's internal rotator, so it is loaded eccentrically at the end of the cocking phase.

q: A client reports calf tightness that eases when they sit but returns on standing. Which muscle does the attachment anatomy point toward?
o: Soleus, because it does not cross the knee and so is unaffected by sitting
Gastrocnemius, because sitting bends the knee and slackens it at the femur
Anterior tibialis, because it works hardest in standing
Fibularis longus, because it stabilises the arch
e: Sitting flexes the knee, which slackens gastrocnemius but leaves soleus unchanged. A sensation that eases in sitting and returns in standing therefore points to gastrocnemius; check with a straight-knee versus bent-knee calf stretch.

q: Which attachment detail explains why the hip flexors are described as tilting the pelvis anteriorly?
o: They run from the pelvis and lumbar spine down to the femur
They insert on the sacrum, which rotates the whole pelvis
They attach to the iliotibial band, which tilts the ilium
They pull the pubic bone upward towards the lower ribs
e: With the femur planted, the pelvis is the end that moves. Psoas and iliacus run from the lumbar spine and ilium to the femur, so shortening them rolls the top of the pelvis forward; this describes a movement, and resting hip flexor length barely relates to pelvic tilt.
